planting.note: Plant offsets or rooted leaf cuttings in spring into very well-drained, gritty succulent mix; Raindrops needs bright light and an open center to avoid rot.

directions: A Dick Wright hybrid prized for the round, droplet-like bumps (carnuncles) that develop on its blue-green leaves as the rosette matures; the bumps are most pronounced on plants grown in bright, cool conditions, where sun also tinges them and the leaf margins pink. Young plants often start out smooth and only develop the signature texture with age and strong light, so give it as much sun as it will tolerate without scorching. Let the fast-draining, gritty mix dry out completely between waterings and keep water out of the rosette center to prevent rot. It offsets sparingly, so propagate mainly from leaf or stem cuttings rather than relying on pups.

common_name: Dark Vader Echeveria (Plum-Purple Topsy Turvy x Black Prince Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant offsets or rooted cuttings in spring in lean, fast-draining succulent mix; strong light intensifies the plum-purple and ocean-blue coloring.

directions: A hybrid of Echeveria runyonii 'Topsy Turvy' and Echeveria 'Black Prince' combining the wavy, incurved leaf form of the former with the dark coloring of the latter, producing rosettes of plum-purple and ocean-blue leaves that darken further under bright, cool conditions. Tall bloom stalks carry red, bell-shaped flowers in late spring that stand out sharply against the dark foliage. Grow in full sun in sharply draining, gritty soil and let it dry out completely between waterings, since any standing moisture in the rosette or root zone invites rot. Propagates easily from leaf or stem cuttings, and offsets modestly at the base once established.

planting.note: Plant offsets or rooted cuttings in spring in gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun to maintain the deepest chocolate-purple coloring.

directions: Forms a compact rosette of elongated, pointed leaves finished in farina (a dusty, waxy coating) that shifts in color from chocolatey purple toward pink at the tips, with a contrasting green center. Bright, direct sun brings out the deepest coloring and keeps the rosette tight, while lower light causes it to stretch and fade toward plain green. Grow in sharply draining, lean succulent soil and water only once the mix has dried out fully, keeping water away from the rosette's center. Propagates readily from leaf pulls or stem cuttings, making it an easy addition to mixed succulent plantings and rock gardens.

common_name: Dionysos Echeveria (Dwarf Mottled Purpusorum Hybrid, Bacchus)

planting.note: Plant small offsets or rooted cuttings in spring in very lean, gritty mix; this dwarf hybrid is a sensitive grower and resents overwatering.

directions: A dwarf Echeveria purpusorum hybrid, also sold as 'Bacchus', forming a small, dense rosette of thick, mottled green leaves washed with purple-to-orange shading that intensifies under bright light and cool temperatures. Delicate pink flowers appear on short stalks in season. It stays compact and produces few offsets, so it is best grown in very lean, mineral-heavy succulent mix with sharp drainage and infrequent watering, letting the soil dry out completely between waterings to avoid the rot this hybrid is prone to when kept too moist. Propagate carefully from leaf cuttings, since the dwarf growth habit makes it slower to bulk up than more vigorous Echeveria hybrids.

common_name: Black Madiba Echeveria (Contorted Burgundy-Black Ruffled Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Plant offsets in spring in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; intense light and drought stress deepen or bleach the coloring dramatically.

directions: Forms an open rosette of thick, contorted leaves with rippled, wavy margins in a deep burgundy to near-black color, among the darkest and most texturally dramatic forms available. Under intense summer sun and drought stress the foliage can bleach to a coppery orange, then return to near-black once conditions moderate. Bright fuchsia-to-red flowers appear on tall stalks in spring and fall. Grow in full sun in sharply draining, gritty soil and let it dry out completely between waterings; the plant offsets freely at the base and will form multi-rosette clusters over time if the pups are left in place.

common_name: Vampire Red Ball Echeveria (Flattened Rose-Olive-Yellow Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Plant offsets or rooted cuttings in spring in gritty, fast-draining mix in full sun to bring out the gradient coloring.

directions: A compact hybrid distinguished from most Echeveria by its flattened, rather than cupped, rosette of wide, pointed leaves, which shift through gradients of rose, olive, and yellow depending on light and season. Pink-and-yellow flowers appear on short stalks. Bright sun keeps the rosette flat and compact and intensifies its color banding, while lower light causes it to stretch and lose definition. Grow in lean, sharply draining succulent soil and allow it to dry out fully between waterings; it is easily propagated from stem cuttings or individual leaves.

common_name: Tulip Echeveria (Spring-Green Wide-Petaled Open Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Plant offsets or rooted leaf cuttings in spring in well-drained, gritty succulent soil in full sun to part shade.

directions: Named for its wide, cupped leaves that spread open like the petals of a tulip, this spring-green hybrid forms a loose, open rosette rather than the tightly packed form typical of many echeverias. The foliage can take on a pink blush seasonally under bright light and cooler temperatures, and the plant sends up pink, bell-shaped flowers on tall stalks. Grow in full sun to part shade in sharply draining, gritty soil, watering only once the mix has dried out completely. It pairs well in mixed succulent containers against darker or pastel-colored rosettes and propagates readily from leaf or stem cuttings.

planting.note: Plant offsets or rooted cuttings in spring in lean, fast-draining succulent mix in full sun for the most vivid coloring.

directions: A large, colorful hybrid whose broad rosette swirls together blue-green, purple, and peach tones in patterns that shift noticeably with light intensity and temperature, giving each plant a distinctive, almost marbled look. Tall annual bloom stalks carry yellow, bell-shaped flowers above the foliage. Grow in full sun in sharply draining, gritty soil and let the mix dry out fully between waterings to keep the thick leaves firm and prevent rot. It is easy to propagate from stem cuttings or leaves and makes a bold focal point in mixed succulent plantings or rock gardens.
